title: Nancy Wake — the White Mouse the Gestapo couldn't catch
sources: Wikipedia: Nancy Wake (30 August 1912 – 7 August 2011) — born in Wellington, New Zealand, grew up in Sydney; journalist in Europe in the 1930s; married French industrialist Henri Fiocca in 1939 and lived in Marseille; after the fall of France in 1940 she became a courier for the Pat O'Leary escape line, helping Allied airmen escape to Spain; the Gestapo called her the 'White Mouse' for her ability to elude capture, and tapped her telephone and intercepted her mail; her own words on passing German posts: 'Do you want to search me?'; when the network was betrayed she fled over the Pyrenees to Spain in 1943; her husband stayed behind and was captured, tortured and executed by the Gestapo — she only learned of it after the war and blamed herself; joined the SOE in Britain; parachuted into the Auvergne on 29–30 April 1944 and was found tangled in a tree; organised parachuted arms and money for the maquis, dropped nearly every other night; she said she cycled 500 km in 72 hours to reach a radio after her radio operator abandoned his codes; she said she killed an SS sentry with her bare hands; many stories about her come from her autobiography The White Mouse and are not verifiable from other sources; awarded the George Medal, the US Medal of Freedom, the Croix de Guerre three times and the Légion d'honneur; refused Australian medals for decades, saying the government 'could stick their medals where the monkey stuck his nuts'; died 2011 aged 98; her ashes were scattered near Montluçon in central France

Photos (public domain, Wikimedia Commons / Australian War Memorial / State Library of New South Wales / US National Archives / Imperial War Museum): Nancy Wake, 1945 and 1951; maquis fighters in France, 1944; a Frenchman weeping as German troops enter Paris, 14 June 1940; German troops in Paris, 1940; an RAF supply drop to the Resistance; the liberation of Paris, August 1944
Archive film (public domain): 'La Libération de Paris, 1944', filmed clandestinely by Resistance cameramen, 16–26 August 1944 (watermark blurred) — illustrative, not Wake herself
Music: La Marseillaise — United States Navy Band, public domain (played twice with a crossfade)

post.facebook:
The Gestapo called her the White Mouse. Every time they closed in, she slipped away.

Nancy Wake, a girl from New Zealand, was married to a rich Frenchman in Marseille when Germany took France in 1940. She began smuggling Allied airmen out to Spain, flirting her way past German checkpoints — in her words: "Do you want to search me?"

By 1943 the Gestapo was tapping her phone, and she fled over the Pyrenees. Her husband stayed behind; the Gestapo tortured and killed him. She didn't find out until the war was over.

In Britain she trained as an SOE agent, and in April 1944 parachuted back into France — landing tangled in a tree. She ran the money and weapons for the Resistance, dropped by plane almost every other night. She said she once cycled 500 km in three days to reach a radio, and that she killed an SS sentry with her bare hands. Some of it comes only from her own memoir — but the medals are real: Britain, America and France all decorated her.

When Australia offered medals decades later, she told them where they could stick them. She died in 2011, aged 98, and her ashes were scattered in the French hills where she fought.

youtube.description:
The Gestapo called her the White Mouse. Every time they closed in, she slipped away.

Nancy Wake smuggled Allied airmen out of occupied France, escaped over the Pyrenees, lost her husband to the Gestapo, and parachuted back in 1944 as an SOE agent — landing in a tree. She ran arms and money for the Resistance and, by her own account, cycled 500 km in three days and killed an SS sentry with her bare hands. Britain, the US and France decorated her; Australia's later offer she famously refused.
